This article aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the various network analysis tools and resources available to researchers, including those that are not exclusively designed for network analysis. We delve into the numerous software platforms and libraries that support network analysis, such as Graphviz, Gephi, and the extensive Python and R ecosystems, before delving into the various metrics and measures that can be applied to network data. Furthermore, we explore the vast array of visualization techniques and the numerous online databases and repositories that are essential for storing, retrieving, and sharing network analysis results.

Theoretical frameworks in eco-evolutionary dynamics have been developed to study the interplay between evolutionary and ecological processes. However, the time scales on which these processes occur are often not explicitly addressed. In this study, we examine eco-evolutionary dynamics across various time frames, from the deep past to the present day, and investigate how the rates of evolution and ecological changes are influenced by environmental factors. We demonstrate that the transition from ancient to modern ecosystems was a gradual process, and that the co-evolution of species and ecosystems played a pivotal role in shaping life on Earth.

Self-supervised learning methods for speech have shown to be versatile and efficient in various speech applications. However, current techniques are highly susceptible to noise, which can hinder their performance. To improve resilience against noise, a new metric called the hostile susceptibility has been developed. This metric measures the performance drop of self-supervised models when trained and tested in noisy environments. A theoretical framework for analyzing the hostile susceptibility has been proposed, along with a method to calculate it analytically. Furthermore, this framework can also provide insights into the theoretical noise susceptibility of decoders that utilize self-supervised models. Experimental results validate the proposed theory and offer guidance for designing more robust speech models.

The rise of blockchain technology has enabled the creation of decentralized marketplaces, allowing users to engage in peer-to-peer transactions without relying on centralized platforms. By eliminating the need for intermediaries, decentralized marketplaces offer enhanced security, transparency, and cost savings. This paper explores the features and benefits of decentralized marketplaces, as well as the underlying architecture and potential use cases. A comprehensive comparison of decentralized and centralized marketplaces is also provided, highlighting the advantages of blockchain-driven decentralization.

A new method for evaluating the impact of unverified study assumptions on evidence reliability is introduced through the concept of the "E-value," which represents the minimum strength of an unverified assumption required to produce a specified effect size. This approach is particularly useful in addressing missing data issues, as it allows researchers to quantify the impact of missing values on their study outcomes. To facilitate this, a nonparametric model for data likelihoods is developed, and a simulation framework for the E-value is presented. Additionally, the proposed method's performance is demonstrated through its application to a clinical trial dataset.

This relationship allows the quantum plane to be expressed as a quotient of the quantum Heisenberg-Jackiewicz algebra, with its elements exhibiting specific commutation properties. Federated learning has become a prominent approach for training machine learning models in IoT settings, particularly in the Internet of Vehicles (IoV) domain. The primary goal of federated learning is to create a global model that can benefit all participating vehicles while maintaining their data privacy. However, the growth of malicious nodes poses a significant threat to the security of the training process. To address this challenge, researchers have proposed incorporating blockchain technology to support federed learning in IoV settings. This paper provides a comprehensive review of existing literature on blockchain-enabled federated learning frameworks for IoV settings, including an analysis of the challenges and proposed solutions. The paper also highlights the need for further research to address the growing security challenges in IoV settings.

The ELI collaboration, a joint venture between Fermilab and the University of Illinois, is dedicated to advancing our understanding of the beauty and charm quark systems in high-energy proton-proton collisions. By analyzing data from the CMS experiment at the LHC, researchers have made significant progress in measuring the production rates of beauty and charm mesons. Their findings, based on a dataset collected at a center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV and corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 19.7 nb^-1, reveal that beauty and charm mesons are produced at comparable rates to their prompt counterparts. These results are in line with theoretical predictions and provide valuable insights into the underlying physics governing beauty and charm production.

The Department of Energy's Office of Science is investing in the development of quantum computing technology at Fermilab to explore its potential for scientific research and to establish a new research field.  The lab is currently constructing a large-scale quantum platform to investigate and optimize quantum computing and to study how quantum systems operate in real-world settings.  The platform is based on superconducting circuits and is being built to operate at extremely low temperatures, around 10 millikelvin, to minimize thermal noise and to achieve high levels of quantum coherence.  The platform is being constructed using commercially available components and is designed to be easily expandable and programmable.  The low-temperature environment is being provided by a custom-built dilution refrigerator that is specifically designed to support quantum computing research.  The refrigerator is located in the Fermilab Main Building and is equipped with advanced temperature control and monitoring systems to ensure stable operation of the quantum platform.  The platform is being used to investigate the effects of environmental factors on quantum coherence and to develop new methods for improving quantum computing performance.  The platform is also being used to study the fundamental properties of quantum systems and to test new theories in quantum physics.  The development of this platform represents a significant milestone in the practical application of quantum computing and will provide a valuable platform for research and innovation in the field.

This study examines and compares the most frequently employed cryptographic methods in Python applications that have been compromised, leveraging data from the National Vulnerability Database. Our research reveals that the most commonly exploited algorithms are MD5, SHA-1, and unencrypted HTTP, all of which have been repeatedly targeted. In addition, we develop a framework for categorizing and analyzing cyber threats, and use it to investigate the prevalence of specific vulnerabilities, including SQL injection, XSS, and denial of service attacks. Our findings indicate that SQL injection remains the most prevalent exploit, followed by XSS and denial of service, with the National Vulnerability Database serving as a valuable resource for understanding cyber threats.

This paper introduces a straightforward yet efficient method for obtaining high-quality, large-scale, and diverse training data for autonomous vehicles. The proposed method leverages multiple vehicles' collective input to create a reliable and accurate dataset for autonomous driving. By aggregating the input from a fleet of autonomous vehicles, the method generates a reliable map of the driving environment, which can be used to improve the performance of autonomous vehicles' perception and navigation systems. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments on a dataset of urban driving scenarios, which shows that the proposed method can create a reliable map of the driving environment, even in challenging conditions.

We introduce a new reconstruction network called NuSPAN, which is designed to reconstruct sparse signals in nonuniform environments. The network is built upon the Proximal Mean Architecture and leverages the proximal operator of the l1-1.5 mixed norm to accommodate nonuniformity in signal sparsity. The proposed network is evaluated on synthetic and actual seismic data, and it is found to outperform other competing methods in reconstruction accuracy.

We examine the behavior of semigroups of composition operators in modified space of bounded analytic functions, where functions have square integrable derivatives with respect to the Poisson measure on the unit circle. Specifically, modified space of bounded analytic functions is defined as a subspace of functions with square integrable derivatives in $L^2$-type space with a kernel function that includes a term $\log(1-|z|)^{-2}$. This modified space is shown to be equivalent to a space introduced by Bonk and Fu. Key to the modified space's characterization is the infinitesimal generator of semigroups, which must satisfy certain integral conditions. Additionally, the semigroups generated by linear fractional maps are identified as uniformly bounded in modified space of bounded analytic functions based on the orbits' behavior near the boundary of the unit circle.

We introduce a novel method for calculating the Frenkel-Kac-Zamolodchikov (FKZ) scaling dimensions of the Haagerup planar minimal model, a unique example of a non-unitary conformal field theory. By combining the transfer matrix and wavefunction approach, we derive the ground state overlap matrix, which enables us to determine all scaling dimensions of the model. Our findings reveal that the Haagerup model's scaling dimensions can be expressed as $\Delta_n = \Delta_0 + \frac{n(n+1)}{2} + \frac{\Delta_1 - \Delta_0}{L} + \frac{\Delta_2 - \Delta_1}{L^2} + \dots$, where $\Delta_0, \Delta_1, \Delta_2$ are model-specific constants and $L$ is the system size. Notably, this formula applies to both the Haagerup model and its unitary counterpart, the Bondi model, with $\Delta_0, \Delta_1, \Delta_2$ taking different values. Our research highlights the universal nature of this formula, with $\Delta_0, \Delta_1, \Delta_2$ being model-dependent but size-independent.

We introduce a novel approach to assign part-of-speech (POS) labels to words in texts, especially those from older periods, where many unfamiliar word forms make traditional methods less effective. This method assigns a set of probable POS labels to each word, taking into account its various meanings and forms. It involves two main components: a model that predicts the possible POS labels for each word and a system that adjusts these predictions based on the overall structure of the sentence. This approach was tested on the Old English corpus, where it achieved an accuracy of 70.4% in assigning POS labels.

This paper develops criteria for a function to be non-uniform integrable based on the behavior of its antiderivative, creating a versatile framework that can be applied across various fields of study. The theory presented here is a comprehensive extension of existing concepts, including non-uniform continuity, integrability, and absolute integrability, and offers non-uniform counterparts to related notions like $L^p$-convergence, bounded variation, and relative boundedness. The framework is further illustrated by providing examples and exploring its implications in fields such as measure theory, differentiation, and their applications in physics and probability theory.

We introduce a pioneering approach to automatically convert requirements related to cities into detailed formal specifications. Cities are modeled as interconnected networks of systems, each with its own set of requirements. We leverage existing models for city planning and apply them to create a framework for understanding and modeling cities. This framework enables the automatic transformation of high-level requirements into detailed specifications, which can then be used to inform the design and development of city systems. We have developed an online platform to facilitate this process, allowing users to input high-level requirements and receive automated formal specifications.

A major obstacle to achieving large-scale quantum computing is the presence of errors. We introduce a method to counteract this issue, leveraging a phenomenon where errors are "hidden" to reverse them. This method employs a specific type of interaction between qubits, implemented using a specially designed circuit, to apply it to neighboring qubits. We demonstrate the method's effectiveness by employing three superconducting qubits to perform error correction through multiple sets of measurements.

In a general regular category, the connection between a morphism and an equivalence relation represents the smallest relation that makes the given morphism part of a larger, complete relation. This study examines the conditions under which a category can be defined as 1-cartesian, focusing on the relationship between equivalence relations and preorders. Specifically, we look at when regular categories can be represented as 1-cartesian and provide a method for constructing preorders that are equivalent to given relations. Furthermore, we explore the conditions under which a category is equivalent to the category of all preorders and equivalence relations, and we find that such a category must be equivalent to the category of sets.

To better prepare for extreme weather conditions at sea, such as storms, hurricanes, and typhoons, it's crucial to understand and predict extreme weather patterns. Accurate forecasting can help maritime industries and coastal communities mitigate risks and adapt to changing conditions. This study focuses on modeling complex, interconnected weather conditions using a multivariate approach, specifically for three key indicators: wind speed, wave height, and sea level pressure. By analyzing historical data from the North Atlantic and Pacific oceans, researchers developed a new statistical model that can accurately predict extreme weather conditions and their relationships. This model outperforms existing methods, providing valuable insights for ocean safety and navigation.

Recent advancements in vision-language models have led to breakthroughs in a wide range of visual tasks by leveraging large-scale text-image pairs. However, these models primarily rely on matching image and text features, which can be hindered by the differing dimensions of their input modalities. To address this limitation, we introduce VT-CLIP, a new approach that leverages an additional image-text similarity learning module to enhance the model's visual understanding. By incorporating this module, we achieve improved results on various tasks, including image classification, retrieval, and captioning, with our proposed VT-CLIP outperforming the baseline CLIP model on the ImageNet-1K, CUB-200, and COCO datasets.

We introduce a universal approach for generating non-random, random-like matrices from any given probability distribution with finite moments, which can be applied to a variety of distributions including the Gaussian and uniform distributions. Our approach generalizes previous methods that utilized specific operators for particular probability laws. By utilizing this method, we can establish a non-asymptotic, distribution-independent relation that connects the eigenvalues of a given probability distribution with its corresponding quantiles. This relation enables us to bound the eigenvalues of Wigner matrices and sample eigenvalues of large-dimensional matrices in a way that is independent of the underlying probability distribution's specifics.

We identify the segments of the Eilenberg-Mac Lane spectra in the category of quaternions using a method that involves analyzing their homotopy groups. Our approach is made possible due to a connection with the theory of modular forms, allowing us to derive the homotopy groups by examining the spaces of modular forms with specific characteristics. Furthermore, this method enables us to establish the homotopy subgroups of symplectic groups for levels that are not just powers of two.

In this study, we establish the relationship between the tight Hilbert polynomial and F-invariant local rings. Specifically, we demonstrate that a filtered ring is F-invariant if and only if its tight Hilbert polynomial has non-increasing coefficients. Additionally, we investigate the behavior of tight Hilbert polynomials in graded rings, proving that for a sufficiently large initial value of n, the sequence of coefficients is non-decreasing.

The integration of artificial intelligence in healthcare has been gaining momentum, with numerous high-quality research papers showcasing machine learning models' potential in medical imaging. However, the results from these models are often presented in supplementary materials, making them difficult to replicate. To address this issue, the creation of open-source AI medical imaging tools has been crucial. Despite this progress, the lack of standardized data formats for model validation and deployment remains a significant challenge. To bridge this gap, the highdicom standard has been developed to provide a unified format for storing deep learning outputs in DICOM files. Building upon this initiative, we present Highdicom, a Python framework that facilitates the representation of deep learning outputs and structured report content within the DICOM standard. This framework enables seamless interoperability between medical imaging systems and AI models, promoting efficient data exchange and model validation.

A thorough examination of the Einstein-Hilbert action's surface term is conducted, revealing that its associated Noether charge is proportional to the Brown-Henneaux boundary condition. This investigation is carried out within the framework of the canonical formalism, and it is discovered that the canonical generator corresponding to diffeomorphisms encompasses a central charge. Moreover, it is demonstrated that this generator is analogous to the Virasoro algebra's mode operator. Additionally, it is shown that the one-dimensional Virasoro algebra's Casimir operator is linked to the thermal average of the Schwarzian derivative, and it is further argued that this derivative functions as a disorder variable.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have significantly improved the accuracy of identifying DNA sequences, yet existing models heavily rely on sequence annotation data that is often scarce and unreliable. Our unattended learning method leverages vast amounts of unlabelled DNA sequences to enhance the performance of existing models, demonstrating that our model achieves comparable or superior results to supervised models on a range of DNA classification tasks.

The phenomenon of metal-insulator transition in certain materials is often triggered by external stimuli such as changes in temperature, pressure, or chemical composition. In the case of materials with a two-dimensional structure, modifications to their surface can also induce this transition. Researchers have recently discovered that the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ films with a specific crystal orientation is influenced by their surface termination. By using a technique called photoemission spectroscopy, scientists have found that films with a certain surface termination exhibit a distinct pattern of electron behavior, which is influenced by the film's thickness. By comparing these results with theoretical models, researchers have been able to gain a deeper understanding of the complex interplay between surface and bulk properties in these materials.

This research explores the conditions under which a Clebsch authorization can be achieved for a Lie-Poisson system, particularly in terms of its integrability. We derive a set of differential equations that must be satisfied by the authorization and demonstrate how these can be resolved in specific cases. Furthermore, we have two key findings: (i) the Clebsch authorization for an Euler equation is equivalent to a specific connection in the Lie algebra's principal bundle and (ii) the Clebsch authorization for a Lie-Poisson system is equivalent to a specific section in this same bundle's pullback. These results are then applied to specific examples, including Euler equations for rigid bodies and ideal fluids.

Our analysis includes detailed descriptions of the planets' light curves, the secondary light curves of their host lenses, and the inferred properties of their irregular orbits. We identified 12 new instances of planets with non-circular orbits, bringing the total number of irregularly orbiting planets in the Kepler dataset to 24. We introduce an innovative numerical approach for solving the compressible Navier-Stokes equations, incorporating an entropy-stable finite volume scheme and an entropy-satisfying boundary condition. The method is validated by ensuring the conservation of entropy in the presence of boundaries, a crucial aspect for accurately simulating thermodynamic processes. Our approach is demonstrated by successfully applying it to a variety of test cases, including shock waves, boundary layers, and an adiabatic sphere, all of which exhibit good agreement with existing solutions.

The National Physical Laboratory in New Delhi is developing an advanced automated system for accurately measuring the capacitance of individual capacitors. The system relies on an advanced algorithm that uses an iterative approach to analyze and calculate the actual capacitance value of each component. However, the presence of noise in the input data can hinder the system's ability to converge to a correct solution. To address this issue, the researchers have applied machine learning techniques to predict the actual capacitance value of each component. To determine the effectiveness of this approach, the researchers have compared the performance of various machine learning algorithms and assessed the importance of different input features.

We introduce a specific subset of permutations, referred to as "glued permutations," and prove that their associated chromatic polynomials yield symmetric polynomials dependent on a parameter. These "glued permutations" have a natural connection to excedance sets that can be represented as the complement of Dyck paths. Additionally, we establish a link between the evaluation of these symmetric polynomials and the distribution of certain statistics in q-rook theory.

Deep Convolutional Neural Networks have achieved exceptional success in image classification tasks. These networks, however, are not invariant to changes in the input image's orientation. A new variant of these networks, called Orientation Convolutive Networks, has been developed to address this limitation. By integrating a novel operator that accounts for the orientation of the input image, these invariant networks can process any rotated version of the input. Experimental results on the MNIST dataset demonstrate that these orientation-preserving networks can accurately recognize digits regardless of their rotation.

A moduli space of uniformizations for compact Riemann surfaces of a fixed genus $g$ and with $N$ specified points is represented by the space $\mathcal{M}_{g,N}$. We establish a novel expression for the volume of $\mathcal{M}_{g,N}$ through a relative trace formula that combines two distinct representations of $Sp(2g,\mathbb{R})$, along with an integrand derived from functions on the group. Our approach is based on a new geometric construction of the space $\mathcal{M}_{g,N}$, which involves the curved linear interval, a curved version of the fundamental domain for the upper half-plane under $SL(2,\mathbb{Z})$.

The running top quark mass in the $\overline{\text{MS}}$ scheme is calculated numerically up to three-loop order and is also available in an analytic form including three-loop corrections and complete electroweak corrections. The calculated mass is presented in both $\overline{\text{MS}}$ and substantial mass schemes, up to three-loop QCD accuracy. The substantial mass dependence and the renormalization group evolution are also calculated up to three-loop QCD accuracy. The substantial mass dependence is found to be significantly larger for lighter quarks, with the mass difference between the top and bottom quark being approximately 10% smaller than the mass difference between the top and charm quark.
